Description / What Changed: New analysis script (no LLM calls) that turns the earlier interactive artifact into reproducible code. (1) Temporal distribution: per-minute normal vs attack counts across each session plus a 1-second zoom of the first 120 s. The raw data has no date column, only wall-clock time and session-relative frame_time_relative, so positions are in session seconds. (2) Detection-window experiment: the LLM prompt's packet_rate uses a hardcoded k = 4 s window; for k in 0.5-60 s every packet gets a rolling rate [t-k, t]/k on the full unsampled MODBUS rows and AUC-ROC scores how well it separates each attack type from normal. The takeaway box in report.html is computed from the results (an earlier hand-written version overgeneralized, see result summary). UPDATED 2026-09-28: output moved from data_visualisation/ directly into data_visualisation/attack_timing_overview/ (OUTPUT_DIR changed accordingly) so it doesn't mix with the per-attack-type packet_compare_smartgrid_*.py folders; a new build_data_visualisation_index.py now generates data_visualisation/index.html as a hub page linking to every report (session-wide + per-attack), regenerated by hand after each new attack-type script is completed.
Result Summary: Every session: one ~7 s data flood at t~47-54 s (peak 12.1-12.5k pkt/s vs a normal baseline of 8-24 pkt/s); the other 7 attack types are spread across the whole remaining session. Mean AUC across attack types: best window is k=1s for IED (0.907 vs 0.902 at k=4s), k=1s for Smart Grid (0.974 vs 0.955), k=0.5s for WBF (0.975 vs 0.934); AUC falls steadily for k>=8s (k=60s: 0.72-0.75). Weak signal only in IED: force listen mode (best AUC 0.794, n=148) and restart communication (0.777, n=1598). In Smart Grid and WBF both reach 0.94-0.96 at k<=1s (n=16/198 and 36/358). CORRECTION: an earlier statement that these two types are weak at every window size was true only for IED. Small samples (n<50): address scan and force listen mode in Smart Grid, force listen mode in WBF. Run time 3.8 s.
Output Files: overview.csv, timeline_per_minute.csv, burst_first_120s.csv, window_auc.csv, report.html, run_20260919_1701.log

Description / What Changed: New analysis script (no LLM calls, feeds the analyst-prompt work in the Smart Grid normal-behavior-baseline memory): pulls the EXACT raw rows (no synthesis) for one normal fc1 read exchange (master 192.168.0.40 -> RTU 192.168.0.31, mid-session) and 3 representative request/response pairs from one function-code-scan round (5 TCP connections opened by 192.168.0.1 in 21.9 ms, t~549.46s), plus a stats comparison table (function code diversity, write acceptance, reply size, connection rate) against the session's normal baseline. Renders packets.json + stats.json + a self-contained report.html. UPDATED 2026-09-28: stats now rendered as bar charts (grouped Normal/Attack bar pairs per metric, plus a log-scale rate chart for packets/requests/connections per sec) instead of a table-only view, and a dedicated 'Source IP' section highlighting which IPs ever appear in normal vs. attack traffic across the whole session (not just this round) - normal traffic is exactly {192.168.0.31, 192.168.0.40}, attack traffic is exactly {192.168.0.1, 192.168.0.31}, zero overlap on the source side. Exact-numbers table kept as a collapsed detail below the charts.
Result Summary: Round 1 of the fc-scan: 45 requests across 5 connections in 21.9 ms (132 packets total, ~6027 pkt/s), 45 distinct function codes vs 3 in normal traffic, 30 outside the standard public set. Concrete finding: fc5/fc6 (Write Single Coil/Register) requests were ECHOED BACK by the target (i.e. ACCEPTED) even though 0.0% of this system's normal traffic is a write - matches MITRE ATT&CK T0855 Unauthorized Command Message. A fc17 (Report Slave ID) reply decoded to ASCII 'Pymodbus', disclosing the target's software library. Largest reply size 72 bytes vs 63 normal; largest read quantity 0 vs 1 normal.; IP highlight: 192.168.0.1 (attacker) appears in 0 of 47,198 normal packets across the whole session, and the legitimate master 192.168.0.40 appears in 0 attack packets - full separation on the source-IP dimension, not just this round.

Description / What Changed: Second in the per-attack-type series (after XAI-16's function-code scan), same treatment applied to Smart Grid's address scan (attack_specific=1): normal-vs-attack packet examples with charts, plus a Source IP highlight section. This attack tells a different story than fc-scan: 192.168.0.1 is itself a legitimate host (1,252 normal rows, all passive ACK-only traffic with 192.168.0.111, zero SYN packets ever) rather than an unknown IP, so the detection logic here is fan-out (contact-degree 1->6) not pair-membership. Added a new 'Pipeline blind spot' section (2 big-number callouts) not present in the fc-scan version.
Result Summary: MAJOR FINDING: only 0.075% of this attack's 37,306 rows are protocol==MODBUS (28 rows) - the rest (35,183 rows, 94.3%) is ARP, which alone is 98.0% of ALL ARP traffic in the entire 99.4-minute session. Both the AE model and the LLM prompt only ever look at MODBUS rows, so neither can see the actual scanning behavior, only the tiny Modbus tail (a device-ID fc43 probe/response pair and one oversized fc1 read, 259-byte reply vs 63-byte normal max). Host fan-out: 192.168.0.1 goes from 1 normal partner (192.168.0.111) to 6 contacted hosts (5 never contacted before, including the RTU 192.168.0.31), 614 SYN packets vs 0 in its entire normal baseline. Attack window spans 29.5s-5860.5s (98% of the session), not a short burst like fc-scan's 22ms round.

Description / What Changed: Third in the per-attack-type series (after XAI-16 fc-scan, XAI-17 address scan), applied to Smart Grid's 'device identification attack' (attack_specific=3). Reuses extract_normal_pair()/pack() from packet_compare_smartgrid_fcscan.py instead of duplicating. Bug found and fixed during extraction: filtering a round's rows by PDU-value equality to find a request/response pair picked up two requests (the 'basic' MEI code 0x01 is probed twice per round with an identical request PDU) instead of a request+response - fixed by pairing rows positionally (attacker row immediately followed by target row) instead of by value match. Also found and fixed a pre-existing CSS bug in .shared-target-banner (display:flex with mixed text/inline-tag children fragments the text into oddly-spaced pieces) - fixed by switching to display:block; this also silently affected XAI-16 and XAI-17's banners (less visible there since their banner text was shorter), so their report.html files were regenerated too. UPDATED 2026-09-28: user questioned why an unrelated fc1 (Read Coils) packet was labeled the 'normal' counterpart to the fc43 device-ID probe - correctly, since this attack's request TYPE (asking for device identity) has no normal-traffic equivalent at all, showing fc1 implied a direct comparison that doesn't exist. Removed the fc1 example entirely; the Normal column now explains the absence directly (fc43 = 0/47,198 normal rows, normal traffic only ever asks 'what is this measurement', never 'what are you'). extract_normal_pair() import removed, packets.json no longer has a normal_pair field. UPDATED again 2026-09-28: user asked whether fc43 has ANY legitimate real-world use - researched via web search (not assumed). Confirmed fc43/MEI14 (Read Device Identification) is a standard documented Modbus feature used by real asset-management tools and engineering workstations for maintenance inventory, AND is separately documented in ICS security research (Radiflow, 'Hack the Modbus') as a known reconnaissance technique when swept across a network. Added a new report section making explicit that '0 in normal traffic' is scoped to this dataset's definition of normal (continuous measurement polling, no asset-audit traffic modeled) - not a universal claim fc43 is always malicious. The actual distinguishing signal is requester identity + 16-round repeat cadence, not fc43's mere presence.
Result Summary: Unlike fc-scan (one 22ms burst) and address-scan (continuous, ~98% of the session), this attack is pure Modbus (fc43, 100% visible to the pipeline) but low-and-slow: 16 separate rounds of exactly 8 rows (~1.9ms) each, one new TCP connection per round, spread across 5,198.9s (87% of the session), averaging one round every 5.8 minutes. All 3 standard MEI access codes (basic/regular/extended) are probed each round (64 requests total) but the device's fc43 handler returns a well-formed reply with a valid conformity byte and ZERO identification objects every single time - unlike the fc-scan's fc17 probe on the same device, which DID leak the string 'Pymodbus'. fc43 itself never appears in 47,198 normal rows, but is not exclusive to this attack label either (also 18 rows under function-code scan, 16 under address scan) - so its presence alone identifies an attack but not which one; the 16-round low-and-slow cadence is what's specific to this label.
